endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership; PLOS Digital Health (PMID 38723025, doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000390)
endorsements.quote: Solution design is informed by input from both end-users and members of disadvantaged patient subgroups.

endorsements.quote: Furthermore, the respective educational, socioeconomic and cultural background of individual patients and their families has to be considered when, for example, physicians explain PRSs ( Slunecka et al., 2021 ).

endorsements.title: Consensus statement on the credibility assessment of machine learning predictors
endorsements.quote: Education and training: implement educational initiatives to enhance understanding of ML predictor development, validation, and credibility assessment among researchers, clinicians, and stakeholders.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether educating end-users, disadvantaged patient groups, or other stakeholders about inequities and user bias changes how AI is used or improves outcomes. Three sources endorse the practice, a framework and two commentaries, and none of them reports trial or observational data on it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. The three endorsements are one framework and two commentaries, which represent expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply an effect estimate, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The HEAAL framework asks that solution design draw on input from disadvantaged patient subgroups, and one commentary asks physicians to consider patients' educational, socioeconomic, and cultural background. Neither source reports whether education reached or helped Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare bias and inequity education for clinicians and patients against usual practice, with outcomes such as clinicians' reliance on AI outputs, detection of biased recommendations, patient understanding, and differences in care across patient groups. Studies should also measure whether the hazard itself, low awareness of AI bias among users and patients, occurs and how often.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on what form of education works, in what languages or reading levels, or whether it changes care.
